body:
## Why

The operator's call, 2026-09-04: *"I feel like it is much complicated for nothing... I want us to strip the
whole architecture and start with the simplest approach even if it means burning everything down."*

That is a fair reading of the evidence. In the 24 hours to this card, six PRs merged and the reviews on them
produced roughly **90 findings** — and the majority were not about the feature being built, they were about
**interactions between layers**: a driver disagreeing with the interface it implements, a caller reaching
around a seam, a guard misfiring on a worktree, a monitor outliving the store it read. Complexity that
generates its own defects is the definition of complexity that is not paying for itself.

This card is the handoff into that reset. It is not a plan — the plan is the next conversation's. It is the
part that would be expensive to rediscover.

## Where things actually stand (all merged, all working)

- The board is **off GitHub**. 193 cards, 151 run records, 155 results, 173 notes live on
  `refs/kb/boards/default` — a hidden ref, invisible to `git branch`, pushed to origin as backup.
  `hkb list`, `create`, `claim`, `finish`, `sync`, `serve` all work against it.
- `src/store/github.js` is **deleted**. GitHub survives only as `src/bridge/github-issues.js` (the read the
  migration used) and `src/forge.js` (pull requests, which are genuinely still GitHub's).
- One dispatcher, one serve, both healthy. `hkb doctor` is clean apart from two known warnings.
- **In review, unmerged: #296** (the runtime seam) — 11 review findings outstanding, none applied.

## What is load-bearing, and why — the part worth not re-deriving

Keep these regardless of how small the rewrite goes. Each one cost something to learn:

1. **A claim must be a compare-and-swap, and liveness must be a heartbeat.** Everything else about worker
   management is negotiable; this is not. Two workers on one card corrupts the branch.
2. **A hand-claimed attempt has no pid, so liveness for it comes from the heartbeat alone.** This exact rule
   has been dropped by a refactor **twice** and both times the reclaim chain started killing live work after
   180 s (ADR-004 records the first; I restored it again on 2026-09-03).
3. **A board read that returns nothing is a board that could not be read — never a board where everything is
   done.** `gc` treated an empty read as "all finished" and destroyed worker worktrees *with uncommitted work
   in them*. Reproduced, then fixed.
4. **A ref outside `refs/heads` gets no reflog unless you pass `--create-reflog`.** The durable tier silently
   lost its recovery record when it moved to a hidden ref.
5. **A fetch refspec must map into a namespace of your own** (`refs/kb/remotes/...`), not into
   `refs/remotes/`, where a remote branch named `kb` makes it a directory/file conflict that breaks
   `git fetch` for the whole repository. Measured against the real remote.
6. **`archive` closes a card `not_planned` unless it was already `done`, and `blockerDone` rejects
   `not_planned`** — so archiving a superseded card silently freezes everything behind it.
7. **Silent monitors are the recurring failure of this system.** Three in one session: a dispatcher that
   exited and nothing said so (#336), a web board serving a pre-migration snapshot for hours, and
   `hkb watch` still polling GitHub after the store retired (#337). Each looked exactly like a quiet board.

## What I would burn, if asked

Not a recommendation the next conversation has to take — just the honest read from having reviewed all of it:

- **Two ways to launch a Claude worker** (`process` and `claude-bg`). `claude-bg` is arm's-length to a
  session daemon and produced most of the operational pain: a socket death that cost an hour, `claude stop`
  / `claude rm` / worktree cleanup on every recovery, `KB_TASK` not reaching the session so identity has to
  come from the worktree path, and #310's models ignored because there is no launch line to carry them.
- **The GitHub-shaped vocabulary that survived the migration** — labels, issue numbers, `Closes #n` — now
  that cards are files on a ref.
- **Tracks** (a root plus its subgraph in one session) as a *default*. It has withdrawn or misfired three
  times in this session alone and needed `--off` each time.
- Possibly **profiles + capabilities + tool grants** as three separate concepts.

And the thing worth keeping even in a burn-down, because it is what made the migration survivable: **one
interface with a conformance suite two implementations both had to pass.** It is what caught the driver
disagreements that a green test suite did not.

## Open, undecided

- **#296 in review, 11 findings**: the seam is declared but callers still reach around it — the tick asks
  "is this alive", gets the right answer, then ignores it and applies a `claude-bg`-shaped test to the raw
  handle. Relevant only if a seam survives the reset.
- **The SDK** (#312): researched against the docs on 2026-09-04. Per-subagent `model` **is** honoured, so
  #310 is hkb's own gap. Sessions are per-process by design. **Bundling is not supported** — the SDK uses
  `import.meta.url` to find its CLI and bundlers break it. So an SDK runtime is a real dependency, not one
  that can be vendored away, and "zero npm dependencies" has to be amended or the SDK stays optional.
- Whether `manual` (a human claiming a card and doing the work) is a peer of a harness adapter or a
  degenerate case of one. The operator's instinct is that it is not a peer; the counter-evidence is item 2
  above — as a special case it has been deleted twice.

## Done when

This card closes when the next architecture is decided and filed. It is a handoff, not work.
title: RESET: strip the architecture — state, what is load-bearing, and what cost real time to learn
